analysis.one_liner: Bans discrimination against people with disabilities in jobs, public services, businesses, transportation, and telecommunications.
analysis.headline: The House passed the Americans with Disabilities Act 403-20 on May 22, 1990, and its text became the law signed that July.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill makes discrimination against people with disabilities illegal in four big areas: jobs, state and local government services, private businesses open to the public, and telephone service. Employers with 15 or more workers must provide reasonable accommodations unless it would cause undue hardship; new buses, rail cars, and buildings must be accessible; and phone companies must offer relay services so deaf and speech-impaired people can make calls. It also gives people who face discrimination the right to sue, with attorney's fees available.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 43 million Americans with disabilities identified in the bill's findings gain enforceable civil rights: protection from being fired or not hired because of a disability, the right to reasonable accommodations at work, access to state and local government programs and transit, entry to restaurants, hotels, and stores, and telephone relay services. Their families and associates are also protected from discrimination by association.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with disabilities, about 43 million Americans

how_it_helps.text: Employers with 15 or more employees, employment agencies, and unions can no longer refuse to hire, fire, or pay less because of a disability, and must make reasonable accommodations — accessible facilities, modified schedules, equipment, interpreters — unless doing so would impose undue hardship on the business. The enforcement machinery of the 1964 Civil Rights Act applies.

State and local governments can no longer exclude disabled people from their programs, and transit agencies must buy accessible new buses and rail cars, run paratransit service for people who cannot use fixed-route buses, and make key rail stations accessible — with extensions of up to 20 years only for extraordinarily expensive structural changes.

Restaurants, hotels, stores, doctors' offices, theaters, and other places of public accommodation must remove architectural barriers where it is readily achievable, modify policies, and provide auxiliary aids; new construction must be accessible, and alterations must make the changed area and its path of travel accessible.

Telephone companies must provide relay services 24 hours a day, every day, at rates no higher than voice calls, so people who are deaf, hard of hearing, or speech-impaired can communicate by phone; the FCC enforces this with penalties of $10,000 per knowing violation.

People who face discrimination get practical tools to enforce their rights: lawsuits under established civil rights procedures, reasonable attorney's fees, and a waiver of state immunity so states can be sued for violations.

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers, small businesses open to the public, state and local transit agencies, and telephone companies bear the compliance costs — accommodations at work, barrier removal and accessible new construction, accessible vehicles and paratransit, and relay services. Some of these costs pass through to customers and taxpayers, and losing parties may owe attorney's fees in lawsuits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Covered employers, businesses, transit agencies, phone companies

drawbacks.text: The compliance costs are real and fall hardest on small operations: removing architectural barriers where 'readily achievable,' accommodating workers, and, for transit agencies, buying accessible fleets and running paratransit. The bill tries to soften this with defenses — undue hardship, business necessity, direct threat to safety — and long timelines, but the cost of access is borne by the businesses and governments that previously ignored it.
The attorney's fees provision rewards litigation, which critics argued would generate lawsuits against small businesses over vague standards like 'readily achievable.'

The bill concedes significant carve-outs: restaurants may refuse to assign a person with an infectious or communicable disease of public-health significance to a food-handling job (with alternative employment offered), current illegal drug users are excluded from protection, and homosexuality, bisexuality, compulsive gambling, kleptomania, and similar conditions are expressly removed from the definition of disability.

Access to existing rail stations is not immediate: the deadline for key stations can be stretched by the Transportation Secretary up to 20 years for extraordinarily expensive structural changes, so some disabled riders waited decades for accessible stations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and civil-rights-scale — employment, mobility, and basic access to public life for tens of millions of people — while the costs, though genuine, were deliberately tempered in the bill itself: 'reasonable' accommodation, 'readily achievable' barrier removal, undue-hardship and business-necessity defenses, paratransit rather than full fleet conversion, and 20-year extensions for the most expensive station retrofits. The main honest criticism is litigation exposure for small businesses under vaguely defined standards, and the law's carve-outs for food handling, drug users, and certain conditions show how much was bargained away to get 403 votes.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 403-20, then set its own version aside in favor of the Senate bill S. 933, which carried the House text to enactment as the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, signed into law that summer.

narrative.text: Rep. Tony Coelho introduced the bill on May 9, 1989, and it was referred simultaneously to four committees: Education and Labor, Energy and Commerce, Public Works and Transportation, and Judiciary.

The committees and their subcommittees held extensive hearings through 1989 — including field hearings in Houston and Indianapolis — and marked the bill up repeatedly, with the EEOC submitting favorable comments; all four committees reported it amended in May 1990.

A Republican motion to recommit — which would have let employers consider a worker's drug and alcohol history, time in recovery, and treatment before assigning safety-sensitive jobs — failed 143-280, with 135 of 176 voting Republicans in favor and only 8 of 256 voting Democrats.
On May 22, 1990, the House passed the bill 403-20, with 248 of 256 voting Democrats and 155 of 176 voting Republicans in favor.

Rather than go to conference with its own version, the House laid H.R. 2273 on the table and forwarded its text through the Senate companion bill S. 933, which became the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 — the law President George H.W. Bush signed on July 26, 1990.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Americans with disabilities came out ahead: they gained enforceable rights in jobs, government services, transit, businesses, and telephone service, with negotiated compliance timelines that gave businesses and transit agencies years to adapt rather than an abrupt shock.

sides.party_line_note: Passage was 403-20, with 248 of 256 voting Democrats and 155 of 176 voting Republicans in favor; the sharpest party split came on the failed Republican motion to recommit, 135 of 176 voting Republicans for it versus 8 of 256 voting Democrats.

industries.note: The bill imposes a duty not to discriminate and to provide reasonable accommodations, with attorney's fees for prevailing workers. The industry's interest in avoiding these obligations runs against workers' right to access; the law's business-necessity and undue-hardship defenses, and access to a wider labor pool, are the offsets.

Agencies must buy only accessible new buses and rail cars, provide paratransit comparable to fixed-route service, and make key rail stations accessible — with extensions up to 20 years for extraordinarily expensive structural changes. Riders with disabilities gain mobility that agencies had not provided on their own.

industries.industry: Restaurants, retail, and other public accommodations
industries.note: These businesses must remove barriers where readily achievable, make reasonable policy changes, and build new construction to accessible standards. The food-handling exception for people with infectious diseases shows the industry negotiated protections into the bill.

Every common carrier offering voice service must provide 24/7 relay services at rates no higher than voice calls, with $10,000 penalties per knowing violation. Deaf and speech-impaired customers gain phone access at carriers' expense.

The mandate that all new fixed-route buses and rail cars be accessible creates a guaranteed market for lift-equipped and accessible vehicles; their interest in selling more vehicles runs alongside the public's interest in accessible transit.
